The affected brands span six internet service providers riding on that one backend: STNet, KDDI Web Communications, JCOM, Chubu Telecommunications, Nifty, and Biglobe. A customer of any of them could be exposed without ever having signed up with KDDI directly.

The root cause, per KDDI, was a vulnerability in third-party software used in the email platform. The company hasn't named the product. What the incident really illustrates is consolidation risk. When six consumer ISPs share one mail backend, a single bug in one dependency becomes a breach across all six brands at once. That's efficient until the day it isn't.

KDDI says it has modified the affected system, is working with the impacted ISPs to notify users, and is cooperating with Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. The 14.2 million figure is an upper bound on accounts that could be affected, not a confirmed count of compromised credentials. The investigation is ongoing.

If you hold mail at any of those six providers, change the password now and change it anywhere you reused it. Email passwords are reset-everything passwords. Whoever has them can pivot into every account that uses that address for recovery, which is the real reason a mail breach is worse than the headline number suggests.

item.title: The 'Tokenmaxxing' Era Is Ending as Companies Rein In AI Bills
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Enterprises that told staff to burn as many tokens as possible are now demanding ROI, and some are routing traffic to cheaper models.
item.content:encoded:
Uber went through its entire annual AI budget in four months. The company's CTO, Praveen Neppalli Naga, told The Information as much earlier this year, and the response was the tell: Uber put spending tiers on some AI tools, starting at a $1,500-per-month base, with employees having to request anything above that. When a company that size starts metering token use like an overage plan, the mood has shifted.

The thing that's ending has a name. "Tokenmaxxing" was the brief period where employers told developers to use as much AI as humanly possible and treated raw token consumption as a stand-in for productivity. More tokens meant more innovation, supposedly. For a year that logic held, because the spending was a land grab and nobody wanted to be the team that under-invested.

Now the same leaders want receipts. Tighter controls, clearer return on investment, and cheaper alternatives where the expensive model isn't earning its keep. The most pointed example: the CEO of the AI startup Lindy moved all of his company's traffic off Anthropic's Claude and onto DeepSeek, the cheaper Chinese open-weight option, and watched the cost curve fall off a cliff. That's not a rounding-error saving. That's a different bill.

The timing is awkward for the two biggest labs. OpenAI and Anthropic both filed confidentially for what could be historic IPOs in early June, right as their largest enterprise customers start asking why the monthly invoice keeps climbing. Models like Zhipu's GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek give those customers a credible threat to walk, and a credible threat is all you need to renegotiate.

None of this means demand for AI is shrinking. It means the era of unmetered, ROI-optional spending is over, and the providers that win the next phase will be the ones whose pricing survives a CFO actually reading the line items.

item.title: Zhipu's GLM-5.2 Is the First Open-Weight Model That Feels Frontier
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: China's Zhipu shipped MIT-licensed weights that land within a point of Claude Opus on an agentic benchmark at roughly a fifth of the price.
item.content:encoded:
For two years the open-weight crowd has had to settle for "good enough." GLM-5.2, from the Chinese lab Zhipu, is the model that stops the apologizing. Released under a full MIT license on June 17, it scores within about a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on a widely cited agentic benchmark, and it does it at roughly a fifth of the cost. Practitioners who've actually run it, not just read the chart, keep describing it the same way: the first open model that feels plausibly frontier in daily use.

The numbers behind that have texture. It's a mixture-of-experts model, 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active per token, and the context window has been stretched to one million tokens. On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, GLM-5.2 lands at 51, ahead of MiniMax-M3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro at 44 and Kimi K2.6 at 43. That ordering matters less than the gap it closes: the best open model is now trading blows with the closed ones rather than chasing them by a generation.

The price is the headline for anyone running real workloads. Through a host like OpenRouter, GLM-5.2 runs around $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output. GPT-5.5 sits at roughly $5 and $30. Claude Opus is near $5 and $25. When a model is one-fifth the cost and a rounding error behind on quality, the math starts making the decision for you.

There's a real distinction worth keeping straight, though. Open weights mean you can download GLM-5.2 and run it on your own hardware, where your data never leaves your network. Calling Zhipu's hosted API is a different deal, and sending sensitive prompts to a Chinese-operated endpoint carries the data-governance questions you'd expect. The benchmark wins are also benchmark wins. A score of 51 doesn't tell you how it handles your codebase or your weird internal tooling, and the only way to know is to try it.

The timing stings for the US labs. CNBC framed it bluntly this week: Zhipu is closing in while OpenAI and Anthropic are partly held back by Washington's release controls. A capable model you can host yourself, license freely, and run cheap is exactly the thing that erodes a premium API's pricing power. That pressure is already showing up in how companies budget for AI.

item.title: Google Patches Its Fifth Chrome Zero-Day of 2026, Already Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-11645 is an out-of-bounds memory bug in Chrome's V8 engine that attackers were exploiting before the fix shipped.
item.content:encoded:
Five. That's how many actively exploited Chrome zero-days Google has patched since January, and the count is only half the year. The latest is CVE-2026-11645, an out-of-bounds memory access in V8, the JavaScript and WebAssembly engine that does the heavy lifting on every page you open. Google says plainly that it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-11645 exists in the wild."

An out-of-bounds bug in V8 is the kind attackers like because it's reachable from a web page. A crafted site corrupts memory inside the engine and, chained with the right follow-on, becomes code running in the browser's context. The flaw is rated high severity, with a CVSS of 8.8 in the public scoring. The fix lands in Chrome 149.0.7827.102 for Windows and Linux and 149.0.7827.103 for Mac.

An anonymous researcher reported the bug to Google a couple of weeks before the patch shipped, reportedly earning a five-figure bounty. The faster turnaround between a private report and an in-the-wild exploit is becoming the pattern, and it isn't an accident. Google and Microsoft have both pointed to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a reason patch volumes keep climbing. Microsoft's June update alone topped 200 CVEs. More eyes, human and machine, on the same memory-safety bugs means more of them surface at once.

This isn't a Chrome-only problem either. Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi all ride on Chromium and inherit V8, so they're exposed until each ships the same fix. If you maintain any of those in a fleet, they're on your list too.

Updating takes ten seconds and most people skip it anyway. Open the menu, go to Help, click About Google Chrome, and let it pull the update, then hit Relaunch. The fix does nothing sitting in a tab you never restarted.

item.title: ShinyHunters Hit 100+ PeopleSoft Servers Through an Oracle Zero-Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-35273 let attackers run code on PeopleSoft with no login, and Mandiant says two-thirds of the affected organizations are universities.
item.content:encoded:
The calling card was a file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT, dropped into PeopleSoft directories after the attackers had already taken what they came for. The crew behind it is ShinyHunters, and the way in was CVE-2026-35273, a remote code execution flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools rated 9.8 out of 10. No login required, no user interaction, just network access over HTTP to a vulnerable instance.

The bug lives in the Updates Environment Management component, the piece behind the Environment Management Hub known as PSEMHUB. Mandiant dated the activity to a window between May 27 and June 9. Oracle didn't publish its out-of-band advisory until June 10, which means it was a true zero-day the entire time attackers were working through it.

Mandiant, now part of Google, notified more than 100 organizations whose internet-facing endpoints matched the vulnerable fingerprint. Roughly 68 percent of them are in higher education, most in the United States. Some blocked the activity in time. Others were compromised and watched their data land on the ShinyHunters leak site, with the University of Nottingham among the first confirmed victims.

The post-exploitation work was unglamorous and effective. After landing on a PeopleSoft host, the attackers sprayed a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords over SSH to reach other internal machines, compressed stolen data with zstd, and shipped it out over an SSH connection to the server hosting a public mirror of their leak site. Nothing here is exotic. It's a known group running a clean playbook against a class of systems that universities and large enterprises run wide open for staff and student self-service.

If you run PeopleSoft, the PeopleTools patch from Oracle's June 10 alert is the floor, not the ceiling. Assume anything reachable before you patched may already be compromised, hunt for that marker file and unexpected SSH activity between PeopleSoft hosts, and reset the credentials that were sitting on those servers. The leak-site postings are still trickling out, so the list of named victims isn't final.

item.title: Self-Spreading Miasma Worm Poisons 20+ npm Packages in Seconds
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A hijacked maintainer account pushed credential-stealing updates to Leo Platform and RStreams packages, and the malware republishes itself to spread.
item.content:encoded:
The whole thing took under three seconds. Late on June 24, an attacker who had taken over the npm maintainer account "czirker" pushed poisoned updates to more than 20 packages used by the Leo Platform and RStreams data-streaming projects. There was no human at the keyboard timing it. The publish run was fully automated, which is how you compromise two dozen package versions faster than most people can read a single changelog.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence flagged the campaign, with extra technical analysis from Sonatype. The malware family is called Miasma, and it does two things well. First, it hunts for secrets: AWS, Azure and GCP credentials, GitHub tokens, Kubernetes secrets, HashiCorp Vault access, 1Password data, and the victim's own npm publishing tokens. Second, and this is the part that makes it dangerous, it uses those stolen npm tokens to republish itself into more packages. It's a worm. Steal a maintainer's keys, ship a tainted version under their name, harvest the next maintainer's keys, repeat.

If that pattern sounds familiar, it should. Miasma is the same lineage as the Shai-Hulud self-propagating npm attacks, and a "mini Shai-Hulud" toolkit went public on GitHub earlier this month, lowering the bar for anyone who wants to run this play. Miasma also showed up at the start of June in the @redhat-cloud-services compromise, where a hijacked Red Hat employee GitHub account was used to push malicious orphan commits into RedHatInsights repositories, poisoning around 32 packages that pulled roughly 80,000 weekly downloads between them.

The uncomfortable detail in the Red Hat case was that the malicious commits bypassed code review entirely. The June 24 round skips review too, because once an attacker holds a publishing token, npm just accepts the upload. Two-factor authentication on the human login doesn't help when the token is what's being abused.

For anyone shipping software, the move is the boring one that works: pin dependencies to known-good versions, turn on npm's granular access tokens with the shortest viable lifetime, and audit your lockfile for any package that updated in the last few days across the Leo Platform or RStreams trees. If a build pulled a poisoned version, treat every credential that touched that build host as burned and rotate it. The worm's entire business model is the credentials you didn't rotate fast enough.

item.title: CISA Adds PTC Windchill RCE to KEV as Webshells Land on PLM Servers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-12569 is a CVSS 10.0 deserialization bug in Windchill and FlexPLM, and CISA confirmed active exploitation by adding it to the KEV catalog on June 25.
item.content:encoded:
A perfect-10 remote code execution bug in PTC's Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management suites is being exploited in the wild, and CISA added CVE-2026-12569 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 25. Federal agencies now have a hard deadline to patch, and everyone else should treat that date as their own.

The flaw is an unsafe deserialization of untrusted data, the kind of bug that turns a web request into arbitrary code on the server. No authentication is required. PTC rates it CVSS 10.0, Germany's BSI issued its own critical warning, and the affected footprint includes Windchill's PDMLink module and FlexPLM, the systems that hold a manufacturer's CAD files, bills of materials, and product specs.

What makes this one worth your attention is who runs Windchill. It's the engineering backbone for aerospace, automotive, industrial, and defense suppliers. A webshell on a PLM server isn't a nuisance, it's a window into the design data of whatever the company makes.

And webshells are exactly what's showing up. PTC's advisory describes attackers naming their webshells with 16 lowercase hex characters, so defenders should hunt for any POST request to a path matching /Windchill/login/[16 hex chars].jsp. The intruders also send a custom HTTP header, X-windchill-req, which has no legitimate use in the product. PTC first published indicators on June 18 and has since added more, which tells you the activity is ongoing rather than a single burst.

If you run Windchill or FlexPLM, the order of operations is straightforward. Apply PTC's patch, then go looking for the IOCs, because a patch closes the door but doesn't evict anyone already inside. Check your logs for those JSP paths and the X-windchill-req header going back at least to mid-June, and assume any internet-facing instance was a target.

PLM platforms rarely make the security headlines that VPNs and firewalls do, which is part of why they're attractive. They sit deep in the network, they're trusted, and they're often patched on a sleepy enterprise-software cadence. A CVSS 10 with confirmed exploitation should reset that cadence.

item.title: Three Perfect-10 UniFi OS Bugs Chain to Root, Now Exploited in the Wild
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-34908, -34909, and -34910 to the KEV catalog on June 23 after researchers caught live attacks against Ubiquiti's UniFi OS devices.
item.content:encoded:
Ubiquiti gear is everywhere, from home labs to small-business racks to the network closets of companies that should know better, and three CVSS 10 flaws in UniFi OS just moved from theoretical to actively exploited. CISA added all three to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 23.

The three bugs work as a chain. CVE-2026-34908 is an improper access control issue that lets a remote attacker make unauthorized changes to a device. CVE-2026-34909 is a path traversal flaw for reaching and tampering with files on the underlying OS, including the ones tied to local accounts. CVE-2026-34910 is an input validation weakness that allows command injection over the network. Stitch them together and an unauthenticated attacker gets to root.

The blast radius is the whole UniFi family. Cloud Gateways, Network controllers, Protect NVRs, Access hubs, and Talk appliances all run UniFi OS, so a single unpatched box can hand over the keys to camera feeds, door controls, and the network itself.

Ubiquiti shipped fixes on May 21 in Security Advisory Bulletin 064. Roughly a month later, exploitation caught up. Researchers at PwnDefend reported live attacks landing within days of the advisory, and honeypots are seeing opportunistic probes, which is the usual pattern once a perfect-10 with a public advisory is sitting unpatched on the open internet.

Patch now if you haven't. Then ask the harder question: why is the management interface reachable from the internet at all? UniFi consoles should sit behind a VPN or Ubiquiti's own remote access, not exposed on a public IP. The patch fixes these three CVEs. It does nothing for the next one.

item.title: Mandiant: Cisco SD-WAN Zero-Day Was Exploited Months Before the Patch
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers abused CVE-2026-20245 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager as a zero-day for months, planting a rogue root account before Cisco shipped a fix on June 12.
item.content:encoded:
An attacker uploaded a file called evil_tenant.csv to a Cisco SD-WAN Manager, escalated to root, and created a hidden account named 'troot' with full shell access. Then they did it months before Cisco knew the bug existed.

That's the picture Mandiant painted this week in its analysis of CVE-2026-20245, a flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN that the company patched on June 12. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and lets an authenticated local attacker run arbitrary commands with elevated privileges by feeding the system a malicious CSV file the software fails to validate properly.

The 7.8 rating undersells the operational damage. Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, formerly vManage, is the brain of the network: it pushes policy and config to the SD-WAN Controllers and Validators that steer traffic across an organization's sites. Root on that box is root on the network's control plane.

Mandiant tracked two distinct windows of activity, one running from late 2025 into January 2026 and another in March. In both, the attacker first changed the default admin credentials, then exploited the CSV-parsing flaw to escalate and drop the 'troot' account. That tradecraft, plus the patience to sit on a zero-day for months, points to an actor with a specific objective rather than a smash-and-grab crew.

The uncomfortable part is the timeline. A bug rated medium-high on the CVSS scale was a working zero-day in someone's toolkit for the better part of half a year, against appliances that sit at the center of enterprise networks. If you run Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, patching is step one. Step two is going through your admin accounts and config-change logs for anything you don't recognize, because the fix doesn't remove a user the attacker already created.

item.title: OpenAI's First Chip Is Here: Jalapeño, Built by Broadcom, Aimed at Nvidia
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI and Broadcom revealed Jalapeño, a custom inference ASIC OpenAI says it designed to serve its own models, with first deployment targeted for late 2026.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI now has its own silicon. On June 24 the company and Broadcom unveiled Jalapeño, a custom accelerator built specifically to run inference for OpenAI's models, and the first chip in what the two say will be a multi-generation hardware program.

Inference is the part of the AI business that never stops costing money. Training a model is a one-time spend; serving it to hundreds of millions of ChatGPT users is a bill that arrives every second of every day, most of it paid to Nvidia. A chip designed around OpenAI's own serving patterns is a direct attempt to take that line item in-house.

The technical claims are aggressive. Jalapeño is a reticle-sized ASIC fabricated on a 3-nanometer process, and OpenAI says it went from initial design to manufacturing tape-out in nine months, which the companies call the fastest advanced-ASIC cycle yet. OpenAI also says it used its own models to speed up the design work, and that early engineering samples are already running real workloads in the lab, including a GPT-5.3 Codex variant, at production frequency and power.

OpenAI claims performance per watt 'substantially better' than current state-of-the-art parts. Treat that the way you'd treat any first-silicon benchmark from the team that built it: the number that matters is the one an independent lab measures on a shipping chip, not the one in the launch post.

The structure of the deal is as interesting as the chip. Broadcom handles the silicon implementation and networking, Celestica builds the boards, racks, and systems, and OpenAI gets to point its enormous inference demand at hardware it controls. The companies are targeting initial deployment by the end of 2026, scaling toward gigawatt-class data centers in the years after.

Custom inference chips are not a new idea. Google has run TPUs for a decade, Amazon has Trainium and Inferentia, and Microsoft has its own Maia parts. What's new is OpenAI, the single largest buyer of Nvidia compute on the planet, deciding it would rather build than keep renting. If Jalapeño hits even most of its targets, that's the more consequential story than any benchmark.

item.title: Quantum Computing Inc. Buys a Real Fab in $73M NHanced Deal
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: QCi closed its $73.1 million acquisition of NHanced Semiconductors on June 23, adding chip packaging and fabrication to a company long criticized for thin revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum Computing Inc. closed a $73.1 million acquisition of NHanced Semiconductors on June 23, picking up something the company has been accused of lacking for years: an actual manufacturing operation.

NHanced brings semiconductor and nanophotonics fabrication, advanced packaging expertise, and a team of engineers who build things. QCi frames the deal as its move from research and prototyping toward scalable commercial production, which is a polite way of saying the company would like to ship products instead of press releases.

That framing matters because QCi sits in the most hype-saturated corner of the market. Quantum-computing stocks have ridden waves of enthusiasm that rarely line up with shipped, revenue-generating hardware, and QCi in particular has drawn skeptics who question how much of its valuation rests on real technology versus narrative. Buying a fab with packaging capability is a harder thing to wave away than a roadmap slide.

It's also not a magic fix. Owning a fabrication and packaging operation lowers QCi's dependence on outside foundries and gives it control over how its photonic chips get built, but integration is where these deals usually stall. The test isn't the press release on closing day. It's whether NHanced's lines are turning out QCi parts that customers pay for a year from now.

For anyone watching the broader quantum buildout, the interesting signal is the direction. Several quantum firms have spent 2026 acquiring fabrication and packaging capability rather than licensing it, which suggests the field is grinding toward the unglamorous manufacturing problems that decide whether any of this becomes a product.

item.title: GPT-5 Pro Cracked a T-Cell Puzzle That Stumped a Lab for Three Years
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Immunologist Derya Unutmaz says GPT-5 Pro produced a mechanistic answer to a question his lab had chased since 2022, and OpenAI is leaning hard on the story.
item.content:encoded:
An immunologist fed three years of stuck data into GPT-5 Pro and got back an explanation his entire lab had missed. That's the claim Derya Unutmaz, a researcher at The Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine, made this week, and OpenAI put it front and center on June 24.

The puzzle was a real one in T-cell biology: how does glucose metabolism shape the way T cells develop and specialize? Unutmaz's lab had been circling the question since 2022. According to his account, GPT-5 Pro worked through the dataset and proposed a mechanism, that deoxyglucose blocks the protein IL-2, which would explain why it pushes T cells toward the inflammatory Th17 phenotype.

The detail that makes this harder to dismiss as fancy autocomplete is the second result. Unutmaz says the model also correctly predicted the outcome of unpublished experiments involving CD8+ T cells killing lymphoma cells. If the data wasn't in any training corpus, the model couldn't have simply retrieved the answer, which is the usual deflation for stories like this.

So this is more interesting than the average benchmark win. It's also a single anecdote, told by an enthusiastic user, amplified by the company that sells the product. None of that makes it false. It does mean the honest framing is 'a domain expert used a very strong model to accelerate a hypothesis and then validated it himself,' not 'AI did science.'

That distinction is the whole game right now. A model that generates a sharp, testable hypothesis from messy data is genuinely useful to a working scientist, and Unutmaz is clearly a believer. The work that turns a hypothesis into a result still happens at the bench, run by people who know which answers are worth chasing. Keep both halves of that sentence in view when the next 'AI solved it' headline lands.
